Lecture 3 Processes and Protocols

When we talk about application layer programs we are really referring to processes.

Sometimes processes on the same machine have to communicate.

When two processes need to communicate they use some form of Inter Process Communication (IPC).

IPC mechanisms

  • Shared Memory: OS sets aside some memory to be shared by one or more processes. There needs to be some mechanism to prevent read/write anomalies.

    • Semaphores are special flags that block a process from accessing a resource.
    • Monitors are a higher level construct, like a class, that also blocks a process (see Java's synchronized keyword if you're interested in a higher level of abstraction).

  • Message passing: Simplify communication with a metaphor, create a 'mailbox' or a 'pipe' for messages to be placed in.

    • A writing process will block if the mailbox is full
    • A reading process will block if the mailbox is empty
      • When a message is placed in the mailbox a process is waiting to read, it is notified (moved to the ready state so it may be scheduled to run).

In a networked application, there are processes running on different machines that need to communicate.

Many networked applications running on different machines use a message passing scheme.

A process sends and receives messages through the network with a socket.

IP Address and Port Number

Applications use the IP/Port# combination to identify the processes that they want to communicate with.

  1. IP Address: globally unique address that identifies a machine on the internet.
    • Every machine connected to the internet has a unique IP address.
    • Domain Name System (DNS) translates friendly web addresses into IP addresses.
"http://www.carthage.edu" -> 198.150.93.85
  1. Port Number: this identifies an application, or a process, on a given machine (usually a server).
    • A single machine can have many processes running at the same time.
      • Each process is assigned a port number.
      • The combination of IP address and port number uniquely identifies a process on the internet.
  • Some applications have common port numbers:
    • web server: port 80
    • email server: port 25
    • ftp server (file transport protocol): port 21
    • telnet server: port 23
    • SSH server: port 22

The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) manages port numbers.

  1. Well known port numbers: 0 – 1023. Requires internet draft and approval from IANA.

  2. User registered port numbers: 1024 – 49151. IANA needs technical description of how you will use the port

  3. Dynamic/Private port numbers: 49152 – 65535. You can use these ports for your own applications without approval from IANA.

Protocols

Application layer protocols define the format of the messages, the order that they will be exchanged between processes, and the actions taken on transmission or receipt of a message.

Application layer protocols define:

  1. Type of message (request, reply, etc.)
  2. Syntax of various message types (what fields are required and how are they delineated)
  3. Semantics of the fields (the meaning of the fields)
  4. Rules for determining when and how a process sends a message

Web Protocol HTTP

The web is probably the most successful and widely used application on the internet.

The protocol for the web is called the Hyper-Text Transfer Protocol (HTTP).

The protocol is implemented in both the client and server.

A web page consists of objects.

An object can be a:

  • HTML file
  • a JPEG or GIF image
  • an audio clip
  • a video, etc. that can be addressed with a URL.

A Uniform Resource Locator (URL) has two components:

  • Host name
    • Host names are resolved to IP addresses via DNS (Domain Name System).
  • Path
    • Paths are locations to data on the server’s file system.

A web server hosts, or is able to generate, objects, each addressable by a URL.

A web browser's main responsibility is to display objects on the screen.

HTTP runs on top of TCP which means the web browsers and web servers do not have to worry about packets, routing, or flipped bits.

  • Persistent TCP connection
    • a TCP connection stays open for a period of time in case the browser needs to make further requests from the web server. This is the default.
  • Non-Persistent TCP connection
    • a new TCP connection is made for each object. A client or server can ask for this with the Connection: close header.

HTTP Request Message

There are two primary types of messages in HTTP, request and response.

Request Message Format:

Request Line: Method | URL | HTTP Version \n
Header Lines: Header Field Name | Value \n
\n (intentionally blank line to separate header lines from entity body)
Entity Body: (used for POST requests only)

Actual Request Message:

GET /faculty/mmahoney/index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: ulysses.carthage.edu
Connection: close
Date: Mon, 27 Jul 2026 12:28:53 GMT
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/58.0.3029.110 Safari/537.3

  1. Request line

    • method field- GET, POST, PUT, DELETE (type of request)
    • URL field- path of requested object
    • HTTP version field- version of HTTP that the browser is using

  2. Header lines

    • Host field: host on which the object resides
    • Connection: persistent or non-persistent
      • close means non-persistent
      • keep-alive means persistent (default)
    • user-agent: type of browser- occasionally a server will send different results back based on the type of browser
    • if-modified-since: browser displays and stores (caches) the object as well as the last-modified date. Then, when requesting a page it will see if the object is in the cache, if so it will send a request with this field. The server will send the object only if the object has been modified since the date. Otherwise the cached copy will be used.

  3. Entity body

    • used for POST and PUT requests only. Holds data from forms.

HTTP Response Message

Response Message Format:

Status Line: HTTP Version | Status Code | Status Message \n
Header Lines: Header Field Name | Value \n
\n (intentionally blank line to separate header lines from entity body)
Entity Body: (requested object)

Actual Response Message:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Connection: close
Date: Mon, 27 Jul 2026 12:28:53 GMT
Server: Apache/2.2.14 (Win32)
Last-Modified: Wed, 22 Jul 2026 19:15:56 GMT
Content-Length: 60
Content-Type: text/html

<html>
  <body>
    <h1>Hello, World!</h1>
  </body>
</html>

  1. Status line

    • protocol version field
    • status code
      • 200 OK- success
      • 301 Moved Permanently
      • 400 Bad Request- request could not be understood by the server
        • 404 Not Found
      • 500 Server Errors- server could not fulfill the request
    • status message (reason phrase)- human readable explanation of the status code

  2. Header lines

    • Connection: tells whether the server will close the connection after sending the object. If the data is a large video file the server may want to keep the connection open so the client can request more data.
    • Date: date and time when the HTTP response was created. It is the time that the server retrieved the object.
    • Server: type of server generating the response
    • Last-modified: date the object was last modified
    • content-length: number of bytes of entity body
    • content-type: mime types help the browser determine how to display the object. For example, if the object is a GIF image the browser will display it as an image. If the object is a text file the browser will display it as text.

  3. Entity body- the requested object- html, gif, audio, applet, etc.

HTTP Cookies

HTTP is a 'stateless' protocol.

Cookies are used to track users over stateless HTTP.

Cookie technology has four components

  • cookie header line in an HTTP response message
  • cookie header line in a HTTP request message
  • cookie file on the client managed by the web browser
  • back end database on the server

Web APIs, REST, and JSON

When a program uses HTTP to request data or services from another program, we call the interface between them a web API (Application Programming Interface).

REST (Representational State Transfer) is the most common style for designing web APIs. The core ideas:

  • URLs name things (resources) instead of pages
  • The HTTP method says what to do to the thing:
    • GET - read it
    • POST - create a new one
    • PUT - update it
    • DELETE - remove it

For example, a music service might offer:

GET    /api/songs        (get a list of all of the songs)
GET    /api/songs/42     (get song number 42)
POST   /api/songs        (add a new song)
PUT    /api/songs/42     (update song number 42)
DELETE /api/songs/42     (remove song number 42)

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the most common format for the data in the entity body.

{
    "id": 42,
    "title": "Wires and Waves",
    "artist": "Mark Mahoney",
    "durationInSeconds": 214,
    "tags": ["instrumental", "guitar"]
}

JSON has objects in curly braces, name/value pairs, strings, numbers, booleans, and arrays in square brackets. That is nearly the whole language.

A real request and response:

GET /api/songs/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: music.example.com
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 132

{
    "id": 42,
    "title": "Wires and Waves",
    "artist": "Mark Mahoney",
    "durationInSeconds": 214,
    "tags": ["instrumental", "guitar"]
}
